V:1:0:0: Welcome to Module 1. In this short video we'll cover why you need a licence to drive a forklift, your duties under safety law, and where the safety rules come from.
V:1:1:0: Forklifts work in busy places like this, close to people, racking and other vehicles.
V:1:1:1: One mistake can injure or kill someone. That's why the law treats forklift driving as high risk work.
V:1:2:0: Driving a forklift is high risk work. To do it, you need a High Risk Work Licence, class L F.
V:1:2:1: There's also a class L O, for order-picking forklifts. This course prepares you for class L F.
V:1:3:0: Here's how you get your licence.
V:1:3:1: First, train with a Registered Training Organisation.
V:1:3:2: Second, pass both a theory and a practical assessment with an accredited assessor.
V:1:3:3: Third, apply to your state or territory regulator. You must be at least eighteen, and you'll renew the licence about every five years.
V:1:4:0: Everyone at work has safety duties. The business must do three main things.
V:1:4:1: Provide a forklift that's safe and properly maintained.
V:1:4:2: Give you the training, information and supervision you need.
V:1:4:3: And set up safe ways of working, like a traffic management plan.
V:1:5:0: As the operator, you have duties too.
V:1:5:1: Take care of your own safety.
V:1:5:2: Take care that what you do doesn't hurt anyone else.
V:1:5:3: Follow reasonable instructions and your site's procedures. If you don't understand an instruction, ask.
V:1:5:4: And report every hazard, incident and defect you find.
V:1:6:0: Safety rules come from a few places.
V:1:6:1: The Work Health and Safety Act and Regulations. That's the law.
V:1:6:2: Codes of practice, which explain how to meet the law.
V:1:6:3: Australian Standards. For forklifts, that's the A S twenty-three fifty-nine series.
V:1:6:4: The manufacturer's manual for the forklift you're driving.
V:1:7:0: Good records show checks were done and problems were fixed. Make them accurate, neat, dated and signed.
V:1:7:1: Fill in a pre-start checklist every shift.
V:1:7:2: Write up defect and fault reports.
V:1:7:3: Report incidents, and near misses too.
V:1:7:4: And if you're a trainee, keep your logbook of supervised hours up to date.
V:1:8:0: That's Module 1. Next, read through the lessons, then take the quiz. And remember: if you're not sure, stop and ask.
V:2:0:0: Module 2 is about planning your work and spotting hazards before they hurt someone — including what to do if you hit a powerline.
V:2:1:0: Before you lift anything, think the job through.
V:2:1:1: The load. How heavy is it, how big, and is it secure?
V:2:1:2: The forklift. Can it lift this load, as high as you need?
V:2:1:3: The route. Check the ground, slopes, doorways and anything overhead.
V:2:1:4: The destination. Where exactly will the load go?
V:2:1:5: And people. Who else is working nearby, and how will you talk to them?
V:2:2:1: Use your horn, beacon and reversing alarm.
V:2:2:2: If a spotter is guiding you with hand signals, agree on the signals before you start.
V:2:2:3: On a two-way radio, keep messages short and clear, and confirm you understood.
V:2:2:4: And always make eye contact with pedestrians before you move near them.
V:2:3:0: Two words you need to know: hazard and risk. They're not the same thing.
V:2:3:1: A hazard is anything that could cause harm. A pedestrian near your work, an oil spill, a powerline, a damaged pallet.
V:2:3:2: A risk is the chance that the hazard will actually hurt someone.
V:2:3:3: And how bad the harm would be. A hazard that's likely to happen, and could kill someone, is a high risk.
V:2:3:4: So: spot the hazard, assess the risk by asking how likely and how bad, then control it.
V:2:4:0: When you find a hazard, use the hierarchy of control. Start at the top — the most effective — and work down.
V:2:4:2: Two. Substitute it with something safer.
V:2:4:3: Three. Isolate people from it, with barriers or separate walkways.
V:2:4:4: Four. Engineering controls, like mirrors and warning lights.
V:2:4:5: Five. Administrative controls, like procedures, signs and training.
V:2:4:6: Six. Personal protective equipment. That's the last line of defence.
V:2:5:0: When you work outside, always look up before you lift.
V:2:5:1: High-voltage electricity can jump across a gap, so you don't have to touch a powerline to be killed by it.
V:2:6:0: Overhead powerlines can kill. Electricity can jump across a gap, so you don't even have to touch the line.
V:2:6:1: Always look up. Keep the minimum distance for your state. In New South Wales, that's three metres for most local lines, and more for bigger lines.
V:2:6:2: Lower the mast before you travel, and use a spotter when you're working near lines.
V:2:7:0: If your forklift touches a powerline, remember five steps. Stay. Warn. Break. Call. Jump.
V:2:7:1: Step one. Stay on the forklift. Stay calm, and don't touch any metal parts.
V:2:7:2: Step two. Warn everyone to keep at least eight metres away. Nobody touches the forklift.
V:2:7:3: Step three. Break contact, by lowering the mast or driving clear — but only if it's safe.
V:2:7:4: Step four. Call triple zero and the electricity company, and ask them to turn the power off. Stay where you are until they say it's off.
V:2:7:5: Step five. Only if you must get off — for example, if there's a fire — jump clear.
V:2:8:0: The ground around a live forklift can be live too. That's why the eight metre rule matters.
V:2:8:1: Everyone else stays at least eight metres away, and no one tries to help you until the power is confirmed off.
V:2:9:0: If you have to get off, jump well clear with your feet together. Never touch the forklift and the ground at the same time.
V:2:9:1: Land with your feet together. Then shuffle or bunny-hop, keeping your feet together, until you're at least eight metres away.
V:2:9:2: Don't go back until the electricity company confirms the power is off. Then report it — it's a notifiable incident.
V:2:10:0: A loaded forklift is very heavy. Check the ground can take it.
V:2:10:1: Potholes and cracked concrete jolt the load. Slow down, or go around them, and report them.
V:2:10:2: Soft soil and backfilled trenches can collapse. Avoid them.
V:2:10:3: Cross railway tracks slowly, at an angle if you can.
V:2:10:4: And steel plates, grates and trench covers must be rated for the forklift and the load together.
V:2:11:1: In strong wind, big flat loads like sheets of plywood catch the wind like a sail.
V:2:11:2: If there's lightning, stop work, park safely, and take shelter.
V:2:11:3: On wet or icy ground, slow down, brake gently, and leave a much bigger stopping distance.
V:2:11:4: In heat, drink water, take breaks, and protect yourself from the sun.
V:2:12:0: In a real warehouse, people walk the same aisles you drive.
V:2:12:1: Marked walkways, barriers and exclusion zones keep pedestrians and forklifts apart.
V:2:13:0: A traffic management plan keeps people and forklifts apart, with walkways, crossings, speed limits and signs. Follow it every time.
V:2:13:1: When you're loading a truck or stacking high, set up an exclusion zone with barriers and signs.
V:2:13:2: If anyone walks into it, stop work until they've left.
V:2:14:0: That's Module 2. Remember the powerline steps: stay, warn, break, call, jump. Now read the lessons and try the quiz.
V:3:0:0: Module 3 covers the checks you do every shift, what to do when you find a fault, and what to do if something fails while you're driving.
V:3:1:0: Before every shift, you check the forklift, inside and out.
V:3:1:1: That includes the seat, seatbelt, controls and gauges, as well as the outside of the machine.
V:3:2:0: Do a pre-start check before every shift, with the engine off. Walk all the way around the forklift.
V:3:2:1: One. The tynes. Look for cracks, bends and wear, and check the locking pins.
V:3:2:2: Two. The mast and chains. Look for damage and worn or loose chains.
V:3:2:3: Three. Hydraulic hoses. Check for leaks, and look at the ground underneath.
V:3:2:4: Four. Tyres and wheels. Check for damage, wear and the right pressure.
V:3:2:5: Five. The overhead guard and load backrest must be fitted and undamaged.
V:3:2:6: Six. The data plate must be there, readable, and match any attachment.
V:3:2:7: Seven. Fluids and fuel — oil, coolant, and the gas bottle or battery charge.
V:3:3:0: Getting on and off is where a lot of injuries happen.
V:3:3:1: Use the steps and handholds with three points of contact. Never jump down.
V:3:3:2: Once you're seated, adjust the seat and mirrors.
V:3:3:3: Put your seatbelt on, and check it works.
V:3:4:0: Next, start the forklift the way the manufacturer says, and do your operational checks.
V:3:4:1: Test the horn, lights, beacon and reversing alarm.
V:3:4:3: Run the lift, tilt and side shift through their full range. They should move smoothly.
V:3:4:4: Check the brakes, steering and transmission.
V:3:4:5: And listen for any unusual noises. Write the results on your checklist.
V:3:5:0: If you find a fault, the forklift can't be used until it's fixed. This is called lock out, tag out.
V:3:5:2: Isolate the power. Take the key out, turn the gas off, or disconnect the battery.
V:3:5:4: Report the fault to your supervisor, and write it down.
